items.title: The CBSA classified this business’s golf trolleys as Chinese EVs. Now it’s on the hook for $183K in tariffs
items.description: Joseph McLuckie can’t count the number of sleepless nights he has had ever since the Canada Border Services Agency (CBSA) determined about three months ago that his small business owes more than $180,000 in tariffs on a more-than-a-year-old shipment.
items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[Joseph McLuckie, managing director and owner of JPSM Golf, says a shipment of his electric golf trolleys has recently been slapped with an 100 per cent surtax. (Supplied)]]></media:description>
items._ogDesc: Joseph McLuckie can’t count the number of sleepless nights he has had ever since the Canada Border Services Agency (CBSA) determined about three months ago that his small business owes more than $180,000 in tariffs on a more-than-a-year-old shipment.
items.body:
Joseph McLuckie can’t count the number of sleepless nights he has had ever since the Canada Border Services Agency (CBSA) determined about three months ago that his small business owes more than $180,000 in tariffs on a more-than-a-year-old shipment.

McLuckie is the managing director and owner of JPSM Golf, a small business based out of Pickering, Ont., that sells electric golf trolleys. These trolleys carry golfers’ bags throughout the course as they play.

JPSM Golf has been operational for the last 20 years, starting off in the basement of McLuckie’s home in Leaside before it moved to its 9,000-square-foot storefront.

Instead of celebrating his company’s 20th anniversary, McLuckie is agonizing whether he will be able to pay all six of his long-term employees should he have to pay the $182,883.95 the CBSA says he owes.

“You wake up in the middle of the night, you have a random thought, and it keeps you awake for a couple of hours, because I know if I had to pay this tomorrow, I’m out of cash,” McLuckie said in an interview with CTV News Toronto.

The shipment in question was delivered to JPSM Golf from China in April 2025. It was a 40-foot container filled with 330 Formula remote trolleys, a brand McLuckie’s company designed and developed on their own.

McLuckie paid Canada’s standard 6.1 per cent import tariff on the trolleys and paid a little more than $19,000 at the time.

Thirteen months later, McLuckie said he received a letter from the CBSA saying they had reviewed his shipment and stated the trolleys have been reclassified under a different tariff, subjecting them to the China Surtax Order.

This federal tariff first went into effect in October 2024, hitting a wide range of Chinese-made EVS from passenger cars to delivery vans with a 100 per cent levy that was added on top of the existing Most-Favoured Nation import tariff of 6.1 per cent. Ottawa officially repealed the surtax on March 1, 2026.

Trade lawyer hired

McLuckie said he called the CBSA to see why he was being charged this tax, perplexed on how this could even be applied to his trolleys. He was instructed to file a submission to the CBSA, which he did with the guidance from a trade and customs lawyer.

“The position we took was, ‘Well, first of all, the surtax was intended to assist Canada’s auto industry.’ That means automobiles that are motor vehicles, not things that technically are classified as motor vehicles like golf trolleys,” Greg Kanargelidis, the lawyer JPSM Golf hired, said in an interview. “The challenge is that the tariff classification number quoted on the import documents was the one that’s in the surtax list.”

In their submission, JPSM Golf argued its products are properly classified under the tariff code 9506.03, representing other golf equipment or as accessories to golf clubs, and that the CBSA should permit redetermination of its products.

The CBSA rejected JPSM Golf’s argument. McLuckie raised his eyebrows at the agency’s response.

McLuckie pointed specifically to a section of the letter where the CBSA quoted Merriam-Webster’s dictionary, saying “your product does meet the terms of a vehicle.”

In the letter sent from CBSA, reviewed by CTV News Toronto, the agency did refer to Merriam-Webster and Cambridge dictionary definitions to determine the separate meanings of “motor” and “vehicle” as each are not defined in the tariff.

The CBSA officer concluded the trolleys employ an electric motor for propulsion and are used to transport golf bags, “undoubtedly” qualifying them as a motor vehicle. If a traditional wheelbarrow can be considered as a vehicle, the CBSA officer noted, so can a golf trolley.

Based on previous decisions by the Canadian International Trade Tribunal, the independent quasi-judicial body responsible for appeals of CBSA tariff classification decisions, relying on dictionary definitions is “appropriate” when the terms are unclear in the existing coding system, a CBSA spokesperson told CTV News Toronto.

The CBSA otherwise could not comment on JPSM Golf’s case specifically, citing confidential customs information. With regards to surtaxes, the enforcement agency said the CBSA makes their decisions based on the “legal wording of individual surtax orders.”

“While the Agency does not have the authority to deviate from the wording of a surtax order in its administration, under section 115 of the Customs Tariff, the Minister of Finance has the authority to recommend remission to the Governor in Council,” the CBSA’s statement reads. These remission orders provide full or partial relief from federal tax.

Kanargelidis says the remission could amend the China Surtax Order to exclude items like golf trolleys or, if there’s a remission order already in place, it could be amended to add as another item where the surtaxes are remitted to include these products. He says they requested a remission from the Department of Finance, which could assist JPSM Golf’s case in scrapping exorbitant surtax.

“Two ways to be successful here is to change the surtax order or to demonstrate that the tariff classification was incorrect to begin with,” Kanargelidis said.

The Canadian Federation of Independent Business (CFIB) and Juanita Nathan, MP for Pickering—Brooklin, confirmed to CTV News they have advocated for JPSM Golf to the federal finance ministry.

“It’s basically, what we believe, a misclassification of a product, which is what’s happened here. Like it’s basically saying it’s a Chinese EV when, come on, really,” Corinne Pohlmann, executive vice-president of advocacy for the Canadian Federation of Independent Business (CFIB) said in an interview.

More than 100 remission requests

A Department of Finance Canada official confirmed to CTV News that it has received more than 180 requests for remissions over goods pertaining to the China Surtax Order since October 2024. The official added that the department is currently reviewing another tranche of more than 30 requests “with a view to advancing a sixth remission order this fall.”

The department did not directly comment on JPSM Golf’s remission but noted processing times can vary depending on the complexity of their request.

“Each request under the China surtax remission framework is thoroughly assessed on its own merits by the Department of Finance, in consultation with domestic producers, to determine whether the goods are in short supply in the Canadian market, cannot reasonably be sourced from non-Chinese suppliers, and whether other exceptional circumstances exist that adversely affect the Canadian economy,” the official wrote.

The whole ordeal, in McLuckie’s view, has turned his company into the “unintended consequence and collateral damage” of an act meant to aid and protect the Canadian automobile sector.

“If the purpose is to put a 20-year-old small Canadian business out of business, then they’re doing a great job,” McLuckie said.

items.title: Trump announces sweeping U.S. grab for control of Venezuela’s vast oil reserves
items.description: U.S. President Donald Trump on Friday said the U.S. had entered into an oil agreement with Venezuela.
items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[A local walks past a mural featuring oil pumps and wells in Caracas, Venezuela, Jan. 6, 2026. (AP Photo/Matias Delacroix, File)]]></media:description><media:credit role="author" scheme="urn:ebu"></media:credit>
items._ogDesc: U.S. President Donald Trump on Friday said the U.S. had entered into an oil agreement with Venezuela.
items.body:
U.S. President Donald Trump on Friday announced an unprecedented U.S. push to take control of a fifth of Venezuela’s vast oil reserves, betting that American companies can revive the OPEC nation’s battered energy industry while delivering a new source of crude to help bring down U.S. fuel prices.

Trump provided few details about the agreement, saying only that the U.S. had secured majority control of more than 65 billion barrels of Venezuela’s proven oil reserves through a partnership with private business.

The South American nation’s leader welcomed the agreement, saying it would boost the economy and government revenue.

The new deal would represent a dramatic expansion of the U.S. role in Venezuela’s oil industry as the Trump administration seeks to revive the country’s production and secure more crude for U.S. refineries. Venezuela holds the world’s largest proven oil reserves but produces only about 1.25 million barrels per day, far below its potential after years of underinvestment, mismanagement and sanctions.

Rubio calls deal a win-win

“At my direction, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, and Secretary of War Pete Hegseth, working closely with Highly Respected Interim President of Venezuela, Delcy Rodriguez, and, through a partnership with private business, have secured majority U.S. control of more than 65 BILLION BARRELS of proven Oil Reserves in Venezuela, at no cost to the American Taxpayer,” Trump wrote on Truth Social.

The announcement followed weeks of U.S.-Venezuelan negotiations over a deal that would give American companies long-term access to a group of Venezuelan oilfields and guarantee the resulting crude supply to the United States.

Venezuelan officials are preparing to sign agreements next week granting new oil exploration and production rights to a number of companies, particularly U.S. firms.

Sources have told Reuters that a lease model was under consideration, with fields potentially auctioned to U.S. producers, but the arrangement could face legal and constitutional challenges in Venezuela, where the state retains control over core oil industry activities.

Trump did not disclose the structure of the agreement, the fields or companies involved or how the United States would exercise majority control over the reserves. A list seen by Reuters shows the fields are in the Orinoco Belt and Lake Maracaibo regions.

Rubio described the agreement as a win for both countries, saying on X that it would secure stable, low-cost oil for the United States and help lower gasoline prices.

For Venezuela, Rubio said the deal would bring nearly US$100 billion in private investment, support thousands of high-paying jobs and help rebuild the country’s economy.

Rodriguez, who became interim leader after the U.S. seized former Venezuelan president Nicolas Maduro in January, said late on Friday that the agreement would allow for a significant increase in production through the development of 17 strategic fields and result in tax revenue for the country totalling US$209 billion.

“These investments will contribute not only to the recovery and modernization of our industry, but also to our country’s economic growth, the energy security of our hemisphere, and greater balance in international markets,” she said in a statement.

Legal basis, financial structure unclear

Analysts said they needed to see more details on the agreement’s legal and financial structure before assessing whether it could attract significant investment.

Also unclear is whether the deal will lower gasoline prices in the short term, as developing the infrastructure needed to produce, transport and refine Venezuela’s heavy crude could take years.

David Goldwyn, president of Goldwyn Global Strategies, said it was unclear whether a U.S. government lease would have a legal basis under Venezuela’s constitution and its new hydrocarbons law, adding that there is “no precedent for having the U.S. government enter into a lease to operate oil fields.”

Goldwyn also questioned whether the plan would address the obstacles that have deterred investment in Venezuela for years. “It is hard to see how this kind of arrangement would accelerate investment at any material scale,” he said, citing political uncertainty, an inadequate power grid, limited export capacity and government discretion over the industry.

Since removing Maduro, Washington has been trying to secure a stable flow of Venezuelan crude ​for U.S. refineries while promoting American investment in the country’s oil industry.

The Trump administration is under pressure ahead of midterm elections in November to mollify consumer concerns over rising gasoline prices. Cheaper oil supplies and expanded output could help.

The U.S. also has been looking for solutions to replenish its Strategic Petroleum Reserve, the nation’s oil stockpile, including the possibility of crude ⁠swaps with U.S. ​producers.

Venezuela nationalized its oil industry in the 1970s, putting state-run PDVSA at its centre. Under then-president Hugo Chavez, the government tightened control, forcing foreign producers into state-led joint ventures and later expropriating assets, including projects operated by ExxonMobil and ConocoPhillips.

Under Maduro’s rule Venezuela’s production fell sharply.

Reporting by Jarrett Renshaw, Costas Pitas and Christian Martinez; Editing by Jasper Ward, Caitlin Webber and Rosalba O’Brien

items.title: Quebec election: PQ and CAQ in near dead heat. Fréchette responds to Northvolt collapse
items.description: A new Quebec election poll conducted by Synopsis Recherche for La Presse shows the Parti Québécois and the Coalition Avenir Québec neck-and-neck, with the PQ’s early lead narrowing.

items._ogDesc: A new Quebec election poll conducted by Synopsis Recherche for La Presse shows the Parti Québécois and the Coalition Avenir Québec neck-and-neck, with the PQ’s early lead narrowing.
items.body:
A new Quebec election poll conducted by Synopsis Recherche for La Presse shows the Parti Québécois (PQ) and the Coalition Avenir Québec (CAQ) neck-and-neck, with the PQ’s early lead narrowing.

  • See the CTVNewsMontreal.ca Quebec Election 2026 page for complete coverage
  • What you need to know ahead of election day in Quebec
  • A new poll shows the PQ and the CAQ are neck-and-neck.
  • CAQ proposes to enhance QPIP to allow fathers to spend more time with their babies.
  • Experts say the trade war with the U.S. is changing electoral priorities.
  • PCQ Leader Éric Duhaime says he has high hopes ahead of the election.
  • CAQ announces candidates for Dubuc and Lac-Saint-Jean.

The leaders

  • Coalition Avenir Québec Leader Christine Fréchette hopes to stay premier
  • Parti Québécois Leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon brings party back from the brink
  • Quebec Liberal Leader Charles Milliard promises to renew party
  • Québec solidaire’s Ruba Ghazal enters first campaign as spokesperson
  • Conservative Party of Quebec Leader Éric Duhaime vying for seats

Follow along for the latest updates:

Fréchette says criteria for government aid needs to be tightened

Under fire from her political opponents, who on Friday cited the economic failures of the Coalition Avenir Québec, leader Christine Fréchette finally hinted that she would tighten the criteria for government aid to businesses.

Earlier in the morning, PQ leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon accused her of lying about her true role in the collapse of Northvolt, the battery plant project that swallowed up hundreds of millions of dollars in public funds.

Liberal leader Charles Milliard accused Fréchette of trying to disown her past and distance herself from her government’s failures.

“I think we can indeed tighten the criteria,” she agreed during a press scrum in Disraeli, in the Centre-du-Québec region.

“There are criteria. Points are assigned. They already exist, but we’re going to tighten them. In my view, we need to tighten them further because there are precautionary measures to adopt—additional measures.”

The CAQ leader emphasized that, as Minister of the Economy, she was the one who had ended public funding for Northvolt and Lion Electric.

But she refused to say at what stage of the application process—whether during caucus meetings, cabinet sessions, or ministry reviews—she had reached her decision and decided to cut off funding.

- The Canadian Press

Do campaign slogans work?

Election signs are plastered all over the province trying to convey a party’s message in just a few words -- but do they work?

The Coalition Avenir Québec (CAQ) is going with “Avançons” or “Let’s move forward” in English. The Parti Québécois slogan is “Le choix de la confiance” or “The choice of trust.”

Meanwhile, the Quebec Liberals have chosen “Rassembler. Réparer. Bâtir.” or “Unite. Repair. Build.”

“C’est possible” is the slogan for Québec solidaire, which translates to “It’s possible.” And for the Quebec Conservative Party, their message to voters is “Oser pour vrai,” which means “Dare for real.”

Communications strategist Martine St-Victor says two of the slogans stand out to her: Québec solidaire’s, because it evokes hope, and the CAQ’s, because it focuses on trust.

“And trust is probably the number one issue when you talk about the collectivity of political parties, because less than 60 per cent of Quebecers trust politicians - trust political institutions,” St-Victor told CTV News.

CTV News spoke to people on the street on Friday to ask them what they thought of the parties’ slogans and whether they resonated with them.

Watch the video below for the full report.

- Laurence Brisson Dubreuil and Joe Lofaro

Liberal talk trade, shake off new poll

Voters who are abandoning the Quebec Liberal Party (QLP) in favour of Christine Fréchette’s Coalition Avenir Québec (CAQ) are making a mistake, according to Liberal Party leader Charles Milliard.

A Synopsis poll conducted for “La Presse” and published Friday morning shows that the CAQ has gained seven percentage points while the Liberals have lost six.

Synopsis partner Youri Rivest told La Presse that “half of the CAQ’s gains come from the Liberals.”

When asked by a reporter whether these voters were making a mistake, the Liberal leader replied, “The short answer is yes.”

“Are we really going to have to endure another four years of the CAQ in Quebec? I’m going to make sure that doesn’t happen,” the Liberal leader said during a press briefing Friday in Sherbrooke.

“I’ll make sure that the economic team that will bring prosperity to Quebec in the coming years will be Michel Leblanc, Julie White, Fred Beauchemin, and Madeleine Féquière—not Bernard Drainville or Nicolas Marceau, who have either diminished Quebec’s prosperity or even admitted to making mistakes. We can do much better,” he added.

Charles Milliard is not overly concerned about his party’s decline in voter intentions.

“I think that collectively, we need to take a deep breath. It hasn’t even been 24 hours since the campaign kicked off. Campaigns are useful.”

Milliard stated that a Liberal government would set a goal of reducing exports to the United States by at least 15 percent.

To achieve this, he hopes to forge new alliances with partners in Canada, Europe, and Francophone countries.

- The Canadian Press

QS targets grocery prices and promises to tackle unfair practices

Quebec Solidaire is promising to tackle grocery prices by proposing three measures aimed at major grocery chains.

Since the pandemic, the profit margins of major grocery chains “have nearly doubled,” said candidate for premier Ruba Ghazal during a press briefing held at a grocery store in Sherbrooke.

“While your wallets are emptying, the pockets of the CEOs and shareholders of Loblaws and Walmart are filling up. We must find solutions,” said the Quebec Solidaire spokesperson.

To “lower grocery bills,” QS proposes capping the profit margins of major chains at 15 per cent and banning “unfair practices,” such as excessive price hikes, fake discounts, and dynamic pricing.

The left-wing party also reiterated on Friday its promise to create a network of 15 public grocery stores to “compete with the big players and drive prices down.”

- The Canadian Press

PQ vows to end ‘open bar’ for foreign multinationals

A day after Quebec’s election was called, PQ leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon attacked the CAQ’s economic record at the former Northvolt site, calling failed, “poorly designed” projects like it the CAQ’s “trademark” after eight years in power.

He pledged to close the “open bar” on subsidies to foreign multinationals and instead cut Quebec SMEs’ corporate tax rate from 11.5 per cent to 9.5 per cent — saving a company with $5 million in taxable income about $90,000 a year.

He said the cut would be funded by scrapping the Fonds de développement économique and reducing state “overintervention,” and would also pursue a broad deregulatory push to cut red tape for businesses.

CAQ announces new candidates

The Coalition Avenir Québec announced Friday that Marc Grandbois will run in the Dubuc region and François Cormier will run in Lac-Saint-Jean.

Quebec Premier Christine Fréchette said both candidates are well-versed in international trade and culture, issues she said she aims to highlight during the campaign.

Grandbois has three decades of experience in the arts, business management, natural resource export and public service sectors.

“Based in L’Anse-Saint-Jean, he is well acquainted with the realities of the regions he defends with conviction, the value of work carried out with rigour, and the importance of balancing economic development with cultural identity,” the press release states.

Cormier is a professor of accounting and management at Collège d’Alma.

His areas of focus include youth, professional and economic development.

“Well-known in the business community, particularly for his involvement with OSEntreprendre and his role as a mentor with the Mentorat Saguenay network, François Cormier aims to put his experience and expertise to work for the citizens of Lac-Saint-Jean,” the release said.

Robin Della Corte, CTVNewsMontreal.ca

Election poll: CAQ, PQ neck-and-neck

Voting intentions

Among decided voters, the PQ under Paul St-Pierre Plamondon leads with 28 per cent, followed closely by the CAQ under Christine Fréchette at 27 per cent, up seven points since early August.

The Quebec Liberal Party (PLQ) (Charles Milliard) sits at 20 per cent, down six points, while the Conservative Party (PCQ) (Éric Duhaime) trails at 14 per cent and Québec Solidaire (Ruba Ghazal) at 10 per cent.

Choice for premier

Fréchette edges out Plamondon as Quebecers’ top pick for premier at 26 per cent to 23 per cent, though “none of the above” ties for third at 23 per cent.

Government approval

Quebecers are almost evenly split on the Fréchette government, with 43 per cent satisfied and 45 per cent dissatisfied, largely unchanged from early August.

Opinion of leaders

Fréchette is the only leader with net-positive sympathy (+8 points).

  • READ MORE: Here are 5 issues to watch in the Quebec election campaign
  • READ MORE: Montreal mayor sets priorities ahead of Quebec election

Saint-Pierre Plamondon (-4), Milliard (-12), Ghazal (-17) and Duhaime (-32) are all losing ground.

Sovereignty

Support for Quebec independence holds steady at 31 per cent among those with an opinion on the issue, against 69 per cent opposed, unchanged since early August.

Top priorities

Health care remains the top concern among voters (54 per cent), followed by inflation and the cost of living (41 per cent) and housing (34 per cent).

Concern over instability and the trade war with the U.S. jumped nine points to 29 per cent, driven largely by CAQ voters (48 per cent), far more than PQ (27 per cent) or QS voters (10 per cent).

The survey was conducted by Synopsis Recherche among 1,009 Quebec adults between Aug. 24 and 26, 2026.

- Amy Luft, CTVNewsMontreal.ca

CAQ proposes expanding QPIP

CAQ leader Christine Fréchette says she senses “a great openness” and “a buzz” around her.

“My poll numbers are very favorable,” she said on the second day of her campaign, during a news conference in Rimouski.

Fréchette announced an initial commitment on Friday aimed at families: the CAQ proposes to enhance the Quebec Parental Insurance Plan (QPIP), in particular to allow fathers to spend more time with their babies.

  • READ MORE: Quebec’s next administration facing immigration challenges
  • WATCH: Quebec election campaign special coverage

The CAQ leader emphasized that the QPIP was a “collective success,” but that it needed to “evolve” alongside Quebec families.

In particular, the CAQ wants to extend paternity leave by two weeks and make the program more flexible to better involve grandparents and other close relatives.

The party also proposes to improve benefits in the event of perinatal bereavement.

Fréchette said that an increase in premiums is not necessary and that the program is self-funding.

Trade war looming over sovereignty debate

The trade war with the United States is changing electoral priorities, experts say.

A new report released by National Bank a few days before the campaign began found that Quebec is facing the highest effective tariff rate on exports among all of the provinces.

  • READ MORE: Trump, referendum talk make for a tough-to-predict Quebec election: analysts

It’s a situation that already appears to be placing Paul St-Pierre Plamondon on the defensive as his opponents argue it would be unwise to separate while Trump is threatening Canadian sovereignty.

PCQ has ‘high hopes’ ahead of election

The leader of the Quebec Conservative Party (PCQ), Éric Duhaime, says he has high hopes for the Oct. 5 election.

Duhaime says he expects his party to make significant inroads with voters.

  • READ MORE: Quebec Conservatives unveil election platform focused on ‘pro-family’ policies

“This year is our year. 2026 is the year of the Conservatives,” said Duhaime at the launch of his election campaign in the riding of Bellechasse, where he is set to run for office.

items.title: Alberta, Sask. politicians head to the U.S. for conference, trade advocacy
items.description: Politicians from Alberta and Saskatchewan are heading to Minnesota to advocate for trade and strong relationships at the annual Midwestern Legislative Conference in Saint Paul next week.
items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[A hot air balloon passes behind the Alberta legislature, in Edmonton, on Tuesday, Aug. 18, 2026. THE CANADIAN PRESS/Darryl Dyck]]></media:description><media:credit role="author" scheme="urn:ebu">DARRYL DYCK</media:credit>
items._ogDesc: Politicians from Alberta and Saskatchewan are heading to Minnesota to advocate for trade and strong relationships at the annual Midwestern Legislative Conference in Saint Paul next week.
items.body:
EDMONTON — Alberta Premier Danielle Smith is set to meet with U.S. officials next week, after recently saying she wants to see Canada double down on diplomacy and avoid any further escalations of their trade war.

Smith’s press secretary, Sam Blackett, said the premier had a previously planned personal trip to the United States but will take time out to speak with the officials, alongside Alberta’s senior U.S. representative, Nathan Cooper.

Blackett said in a statement Friday that they will meet with the commissioner of the Tennessee Department of Tourist Development, the head of the Nashville Chamber of Commerce and the CEO of the Nashville Convention & Visitors Corp.

Smith said Wednesday after Canada-U.S. trade talks fell apart last week that the United States had “no excuse for their behaviour” but that she didn’t think Canada could win through “brute force.”

She said Canadians officials need to keep telling their American counterparts that tariffs are destructive and promise to help once they are reversed.

“These efforts include Alberta’s participation in organizations like the Council of State Governments (CSG) Midwest, with MLA Jennifer Johnson serving as Alberta’s representative, and other U.S. missions including MLA Shane Getson’s upcoming mission to the Ports-to-Plains conference in Del Rio, Texas,” Blackett said.

Johnson, a backbencher in Smith’s United Conservative caucus, is expected to be joined next week at the U.S. organization’s annual Midwestern Legislative Conference by six members of Saskatchewan Premier Scott Moe’s caucus.

Saskatchewan is a full member of the Council of State Governments Midwest, while Alberta, Manitoba and Ontario are affiliate members.

The Alberta government said lawmakers from 11 U.S. states are to attend the conference, which runs in Saint Paul, Minn., from Sunday to Wednesday. It said Johnson will be advocating for Alberta’s interests and shared priorities around energy, trade and agriculture.

Saskatchewan Agriculture Minister David Marit said Wednesday he’s among those heading to the conference.

He said he attended another conference last month in Wisconsin, where everyone supported continuing with the Canada-U.S.-Mexico trade agreement.

“I would say that from an agriculture perspective, a lot of the states are onside,” Marit said.

Also attending from Saskatchewan are Rural Health Minister Lori Carr, legislature Speaker Todd Goudy and three Saskatchewan Party backbenchers.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Aug. 28, 2026.

Jack Farrell, The Canadian Press

items.title: Alberta’s current, former premiers offer contradicting views on U.S. counter-tariffs
items.description: On both sides of the longest undefended border in the world, citizens and politicians alike are criticizing Donald Trump’s 'Lake America' order as the ongoing trade war rages on. Follow for live updates.
items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[Alberta Premier Danielle Smith and former Alberta premier Jason Kenney in a combination photo. THE CANADIAN PRESS/ Chad Hipolito/Jeff McIntosh]]></media:description>
items._ogDesc: On both sides of the longest undefended border in the world, citizens and politicians alike are criticizing Donald Trump’s 'Lake America' order as the ongoing trade war rages on. Follow for live updates.
items.body:
On both sides of the longest undefended border in the world, citizens and politicians alike are criticizing U.S. President Donald Trump’s executive order to rename Lake Ontario as “Lake America” as the two nations lock horns in their ongoing trade war.

Experts are urging Canadians to “just ignore” the move, since the order will only apply south of the border. Nothing will change for Canada.

  • Trade War Coverage on CTVNews.ca
  • A list of key U.S. goods facing surtaxes
  • Know first. Download the CTV News App

Alberta Premier Danielle Smith warned that counter-tariffs on the U.S. will inflict harm on both the provincial and national economies. But Jason Kenney, who served as Alberta premier between 2019 and 2022 and was replaced by Smith, said Conservative MPs needed to shift the blame on the trade war to Trump.

Meanwhile, Canada’s latest GDP data shows that the economy grew at its fastest pace in more than three years in the second quarter of 2026, before Trump imposed tariffs on about $28 billion worth of Canadian goods.

Some Canadian businesses say they’re looking to separate their supply chains from the U.S. and invest in local industries.

  • Fierce reaction to Trump’s renaming Lake Ontario
  • ‘Lake Ontario – then, now and always’: PM Carney
  • Canadian economy grew in the second quarter of 2026
  • Canadian businesses and consumers stepping up

Here’s everything that happened on Aug. 28, 2026

Tory MPs should blame Trump for trade war: Kenney

Former federal Conservative cabinet minister and Alberta premier Jason Kenney says some Conservative MPs need to more explicitly lay blame for the protracted trade war on Trump.

“I don’t think that I have seen in their public commentary ascribe responsibility for this trade war to the protagonist, to the person who launched it and sustains it, with belittling attacks on our country’s dignity, threats to our sovereignty and actual practical attacks against our economy,” Kenney said in an interview on The Graham Richardson Show on Friday.

“That’s Donald J. Trump.”

The longtime federal cabinet minister chalked the position of some Conservative MPs, who he did not name, up to the amount of time they’ve been on Opposition benches.

“That’s the old saying, like ‘to a hammer, everything looks like a nail,’” Kenney said. “Well, to a very partisan opposition MP, everything looks like an opportunity to criticize the incumbent government.”

Kenney said the Conservatives need to balance holding the Liberals accountable, especially on domestic policy issues, with blaming the right person for the trade war.

Spencer Van Dyk, CTV News writer & producer

Read the full story here

‘No one wins a trade war’: Alberta’s Smith

Alberta Premier Danielle Smith is warning that Canadian counter-tariffs on the U.S. will inflict harm on her province’s economy.

Speaking to host Todd van der Heyden on CTV News Channel Friday, Smith says she understands the necessity of retaliatory measures being put forward by the federal government, which are set to take effect Sept. 8.

But she says Canadian businesses will pay the price.

“We’ve already done an assessment: $1.5-billion worth of Alberta goods are subject to the U.S. tariffs,” she said. “$4.8 billion are subject to the counter-tariffs that are going to be impacted.”

Smith explains that there are many Alberta businesses that rely on imported materials and intermediate goods to make products for Canadians.

“That’s why I often say no one wins a trade war,” she said. “The best way to get through is to try to get back to the table to get to an agreement, so we can reduce the tariffs as low as possible on as many goods as possible.”

Samantha Pope, senior producer, CTV’s Power Play with Vassy Kapelos

Premiers at odds over leveraging potash

Premiers are sharply divided over whether to use Canada’s natural resources as leverage in the trade war with the U.S., and potash has emerged as a key point of contention.

Canada is a major global supplier of potash, a key ingredient in fertilizers that are vital for the agricultural sector. The U.S. imports about 85 per cent of its potash from Canada.

While Ontario’s Doug Ford is pushing to pull the most damaging levers with the U.S., Saskatchewan’s Scott Moe and Alberta’s Danielle Smith are warning about a harmful long-term backlash.

Federal politicians are also weighing in. NDP leader Avi Lewis called for an export tax on “oil, gas, thermal coal, potash and other minerals to hit Trump where it hurts.”

Read the full story here

Canadian brands turn Lake Ontario name change into merch

Canadian companies are turning Donald Trump’s decision to refer to Lake Ontario as “Lake America” into a chance to showcase Canadian-made products and rally support for the Great Lake’s original name.

Liam Mooney, co-founder and CEO of Jackpine, told CP24 his company quickly activated the Made in Canada supply chain it built for its viral “Canada Is Not For Sale” merchandise, including a new hat this week with the message reading “Lake Ontario.”

  • READ PREVIOUS: Doug Ford calls fan booted from Jays game for wearing ‘Canada is not for sale’ hat

“We were able to activate our Made in Canada supply chain,” Mooney said, adding that the company brought its partners together to say, “This is our lake. It’s Lake Ontario. It’s not going to change.”

Ontario Premier Doug Ford famously wore the “Canada Is Not For Sale” design, and it remains in his social media profile photo to this day.

Meanwhile, Canadian clothing company Province of Canada has launched a Lake Ontario quarter-zip, describing it as a “nod to the Great Lake we grew up on and know best.”

Jermaine Wilson, CP24.com and CTVNews.ca journalist

Read the full story here

‘The America we all loved is gone’: political commentator

A political commentator says he’s “optimistic” about Canada’s future despite the drastic transformation of the country’s relationship with the United States.

“Canada is actually making pretty impressive strides to remove ourselves from American influence even in things like tech, which is extremely hard to do, so I’m optimistic we can escape their clutches,” Stephen Marche told CTV News Channel on Friday.

Marche said the Canada-U.S. relationship has “completely changed.”

“I mean, we are in a situation where American weakness is now in our national interest, which literally has not been true in our country for 200 years,” he said. “Our interests are no longer aligned with American interests…”

The current intensifying friction between the two countries due to the tariffs “is a shocking reality,” Marche said. He recalled that he didn’t need a passport to cross the border until he was 33, about two decades ago.

“But those are the ancient days, and the America we all loved is gone, it’s just a ghost.”

Christl Dabu, CTVNews.ca journalist

Rochester, N.Y., council pushes back against ‘Lake America’

Rochester, N.Y., the largest U.S. city on Lake Ontario, signed a proclamation against any renaming of Lake Ontario.

“We believe that Lake Ontario is Lake Ontario, there’s no reason to change this,” Miguel Melendez, Rochester’s city council president, told CTV News Channel on Friday.

“This is an exercise in futility, and we believe that we stand with our Canadian brothers and sisters in allyship in terms of making sure we protect our great lake.”

Many Rochester residents feel the proposed rename is just “another attempt at trying to create division,” Melendez said.

“The president of the United States is very nervous about the upcoming elections and is diverting all attention to other types of matters to create chaos,” he added.

Joe van Wonderen, CTVNews.ca journalist

No rush needed in trade talks: Union, industry leaders

Union and industry leaders say the federal government shouldn’t rush to get back to the table with the U.S., arguing Canada should use the leverage it has in negotiations.

Flavio Volpe, president of the Automotive Parts Manufacturers’ Association, says while the auto sector is incurring “very damaging” costs due to tariffs, signing a bad deal could lead to more costs and disinvestment decisions.

Volpe says Canada should wait to get a deal that makes manufacturing in Canada sustainable, adding he’s “not worried” about how long that will take.

At a labour rally on Parliament Hill Friday, Unifor national president Lana Payne told reporters Canada must be prepared to “ride out” the Trump administration.

Read the full story here

‘All kinds of nonsense’: former adviser

The most prominent issue right now in these trade talks is a lack of respect and trust, says a former trade adviser.

“We had both back in the 1980s. We didn’t have an easy time,” said Derek Burney, a former Canadian ambassador to the U.S. who played a central role in creating the original North American Free Trade Agreement in 1989.

Burney noted that Canada walked away from negotiations even back then, but at least the countries “had civil dialogue at all times.”

“We didn’t indulge in bombast and insults in the public media,” said Burney.

He said Canada made the right decision to walk away from negotiations and impose retaliatory tariffs after the U.S. would “lie consistently”

He noted that now, “the Americans are going wild with all kinds of nonsense.”

“We see outlandish reactions, like renaming Lake Ontario,” says Burney.

“Can you imagine anything more petulant? And coming from a president of the United States, it is absolutely unacceptable.”

Anam Khan, BNNBloomberg.ca journalist

‘Height of insanity’: MacKay

Former Conservative foreign affairs minister Peter MacKay says U.S. President Donald Trump’s executive order to rename Lake Ontario is “ludicrous” and “another attempt to rile up Canadians.”

Speaking to CTV News Channel on Friday, MacKay chalked it up to a ploy by the president to shift focus from trade negotiations, adding it “seems to be the height of insanity.”

U.S. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, meanwhile, denied this week that U.S. officials were hung up on French language laws, adding Canada walked away from the deal last week “for political purposes.”

MacKay says there are politics on both sides, referring to the Quebec election, referendum in Alberta, and U.S. midterm elections.

“Playing to a domestic audience is dangerous and to the detriment of the larger population, certain sectors in the economy, certain individual businesses, small and large, who are reliant on trade,” he added.

MacKay — like Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre — is calling on the federal government to make public the failed deal with the U.S., and to recall Parliament so MPs can decide together on a path forward.

Spencer Van Dyk, CTV News writer & producer

Manitoba offers $100M in tariff relief

The Manitoba government is offering up $100 million to help Manitobans who will be impacted by tariffs from the United States.

Business, Mining, Trade and Job Creation Minister Jamie Moses made the announcement Friday, saying the province is working to face these challenges head-on.

“We know that the unprovoked attacks from Donald Trump’s administration will only embolden us to take more action to support our growing economy,” said Moses.

Devon McKendrick, CTV News Winnipeg editorial producer

Read the full story here

‘Positive news’ in GDP data, but areas of weakness remain: economist

A senior economist at the Canadian Labour Congress is calling the latest GDP data from Statistics Canada “positive news” as the Canada-U.S. trade war intensifies, but warns there are still areas of weakness.

New data shows the Canadian economy grew at its fastest pace in more than three years in the second quarter of 2026, with real gross domestic product rising 3.3 per cent.

“It tells us the baseline as we go into the intensification of the trade war,” DT Cochrane tells CTV News Channel. “It’s better to have a stronger economy, obviously. That said, there are still many areas of weakness that we need to be aware of, and the government will have to be ready to act if we see those areas of weakness rippling out into the economy.”

One of those areas, for example, is business investment. Cochrane says although it increased in the latest quarter — up 2.3 per cent — it remains well below its highs achieved since the pandemic and remains below where it was before the pandemic.

Cochrane also notes manufacturing had an important recovery in June, growing 0.6 per cent and rising for the third consecutive month.

“We want to see more of that, as that’s where the diversification for our trade really comes from,” he says. “But again, their weakness remains, and so a few months of positive movement are not enough to say we are definitively on a strong path.”

Samantha Pope, senior producer, CTV’s Power Play with Vassy Kapelos

Canada’s economy put to the test

Canada’s economy rebounded sharply in the second quarter after six months of virtually no growth, aided by a strong jump in exports and solid ‌domestic demand. However, the latest round of U.S. tariffs will put that growth to the test. The economy grew at an annualized rate of 3.3 per centin the second quarter, the fastest rate since 2023, after a revised 0.3 per centincrease in the first quarter. Prime Minister Carney’s recent outreach to the European Union could prove pivotal.

Eric Ham, CTV News political analyst in Washington

‘Just ignore it’: expert

Constitutional law expert Kathleen Mahoney said when it comes to Trump’s renaming of Lake Ontario, it’s likely best to “just ignore it.”

Mahoney said in an interview on CTV News Channel Friday that Trump’s executive order applies only to American departments and companies, and not Canadian ones, so nothing will change on this side of the border.

The expert added Trump will likely still have to go through a consultation process domestically to justify the move.

“Even in the U.S. before a name change legally goes through, there has to be a process with the body that is in charge of changing geographic names, and that body requires the reason for the change, the evidence requiring the change, and the need for the change,” Mahoney said.

She added that while Canada could challenge the decision with an international body, there’s little point in doing so.

Asked about the case of Google Maps specifically, considering the popularity of the program, Mahoney said that’s a decision for the company, and it cannot be dictated by the president.

Spencer Van Dyk, CTV News writer & producer

Trump ‘cannot rename away our history’

The Mississaugas of the Credit First Nation say that Lake Ontario is part of its “homeland and U.S. President Donald Trump “cannot rename away our history.”

Chief Margaret Sault made the comment in a statement on Friday in which she vowed that “it will remain Lake Ontario,” despite Trump’s “political decision.”

“Lake Ontario is shared by Canada and the United States, but it is also part of a much older Indigenous landscape. I hope this moment encourages people to look beyond the political rhetoric and learn whose lands and waters these have always been,” Sault said.

“For the Mississaugas of the Credit, it will remain Lake Ontario and, more importantly, it will remain a living part of our homeland and our responsibilities to future generations.”

Chris Fox, CTVNewsToronto.ca journalist

Trump awards medal to Jeremy Hansen

Canadian astronaut Jeremy Hansen along with the crew of Artemis II received the Congressional Space Medal of Honor from U.S. President Donald Trump Friday afternoon.

During the speech leading up to the medal ceremony, Trump described Hansen as “a master of science and physics” and a “great” fighter pilot.

“Jeremy became the first non-American in history to travel beyond low Earth orbit. He documented lunar terrain while contributing enormously to space science and physics research,” he said in his speech.

“And along with Christina, he helped the crew stay healthy and develop standards and best practices. Jeremy, thank you very much. Great job.”

Aarjavee Raaj, CTVNews.ca journalist

Read The Canadian Press’ full story

U.S. figures condemning Trump’s ‘Lake America’ order

Democrats are criticizing U.S. President Donald Trump’s proposed renaming of Lake Ontario, calling it “pathetic” and a “distraction” from failed trade talks.

Trump signed an executive order on Thursday to change the name of Lake Ontario to “Lake America.” The province itself was named after the lake, as “Ontario” is an Indigenous name that means “beautiful lake” or “sparkling water.”

Trump has attempted to rename international bodies of water before, including an attempt to change the Gulf of Mexico to the “Gulf of America.” Soon after signing the executive order Thursday, he suggested changing the names of both the Pacific and Atlantic Oceans.

Democrats are speaking out against their President’s proposed renaming of Lake Ontario. Here’s what they’re saying:

New York politicians

New York is the only U.S. state on Lake Ontario, and its governor said she’s against a name change.

Democrat Kathy Hochul said on social media that the state would not be calling it Lake America.

Her press office said the common acronym to remember the names of the individual Great Lakes, “HOMES (Huron, Ontario, Michigan, Erie, Superior),” would instead become “SHAME” with Trump’s name change.

U.S. Rep. Joe Morelle accused Trump of trying to distract Americans from trade negotiations with Canada.

“Pretending to rename a lake is an attempted distraction from the president’s disastrous trade talks with Canada,” he wrote on social media.

“President Trump is playing games with a map,” he added.

National Democrats

Current and former leading members of the Democratic Party called out the “Lake America” order.

New York’s Chuck Schumer, the U.S. Senate minority leader, called the order “sad and pathetic” on social media.

“Voters will respond accordingly in November,” he warned.

Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders, an Independent who regularly votes with Democrats, called out Trump for cutting health care, child care, housing, education and nutrition assistance in a social media post criticizing the “Lake America” order.

Adam Schiff, a U.S. senator from California, criticized the rising costs of living in the U.S., saying the “best Trump could do is ‘Lake America.’” on social media.

Former U.S. secretary of state Hillary Clinton chimed in on Trump’s executive order, posting to social media on Thursday that “It’s Lake Ontario.”

U.S. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) said “Republicans don’t give a damn about making your life more affordable.”

New Jersey Sen. Cory Booker said he’d rather see every hospital that has closed due to Trump’s policies renamed to “Donald Trump Memorial Hospital,” rather than a “Lake America.”

Georgia Sen. Raphael Warnock called Trump’s rename “a joke” on social media.

Connecticut Sen. Chris Murphy told Americans on social media that “this is why your gas and grocery prices are so high. Because (Trump) spends all his time on this BS.”

Delaware Sen. Chris Coons wrote: “Apparently, Trump thinks the most important issue facing Americans right now is renaming lakes.

The official X account for U.S. House Democrats wrote “It’s too expensive to live and Donald Trump is renaming lakes.” Meanwhile, the Democrat Party’s official account wrote “Facts don’t care about Trump’s feelings.”

Joe Van Wonderen, CTVNews.ca journalist

‘Liars’ in Trump administration: Chapman’s CEO

Chapman’s does not want to do business with “liars,” the company’s CEO Ashley Chapman told CTV News Channel Friday about the decision to convert 70 per cent of its American ingredients.

The company has also said it won’t increase prices until March 2028.

“The Trump administration is proven to just be liars, and they break trade agreements like no one we’ve ever seen,” he said. “So, it was in our best interest to start looking elsewhere, and we are well on track to separating our supply chain from the United States.”

Chapman said the company wants to find Canadian sources that are cost-neutral.

“A lot of Canadian businesses are opening their minds to the possibilities of what they could produce instead of just what they are producing,” he added.

“After this administration is long gone, we will be locked into this agreement.”

Chapman added that the company is ready to “take a hit” on its finances as long as it can make a great product and provide living wages.

Aarjavee Raaj, CTVNews.ca journalist

Trade war hurting business: store owner

A Surrey, B.C., duty-free store owner says renewed trade tensions between Canada and the United States are once again taking a toll, just as sales were beginning to recover.

Peter Raju, owner of Peace Arch Duty Free, said business had increased by about 30 per cent for the past four months.

But now, he says the latest deterioration in Canada-U.S. relations, along with calls from political leaders to avoid travel south of the border, have once again slowed business.

According to Raju, business dropped roughly 80 per cent during the previous round of trade tensions, forcing him to lay off dozens of employees. He believes the latest escalation is already having an impact.

“We have seen an immediate impact on our business,” he added.

Kevin Charach, CTV News Vancouver journalist

Read the full story here

Trump says lake renaming is ‘effective immediately’

U.S. President Donald Trump has signed an executive order to rename Lake Ontario as “Lake America.”

Trump made the announcement in the Oval Office Thursday afternoon.

Trump said the move was “official, effective immediately” and that his administration has “filed all the necessary papers, documents” and “notified all of the various people that we have to notify.”

Kayla Thompson, CTVNews.ca journalist

‘Lake Ontario – then, now and always’: PM Carney

Prime Minister Mark Carney responded to Trump’s executive order on Thursday, reaffirming that no matter what the U.S. calls it, Canadians will know it as “Lake Ontario – then, now and always.”

“The name Lake Ontario comes from the Wendat word Ontari’io, which, appropriately, means ‘the lake is beautiful, the lake is big,’” Carney posted on social media on Thursday afternoon.

“The name is more than 400 years old, predating both the Confederation of Canada and the Declaration of Independence of the United States of America,” he continued.

Carney highlighted that the United States is changing “their trading relationships, their foreign policies, their national monuments and their hydronyms,” but that “Canadians also know that naming reality means calling it Lake Ontario.”

Kayla Thompson, CTVNews.ca journalist

Can Trump rename Lake Ontario?

CTV News’ chief political correspondent Vassy Kapelos answered the question on a lot of Canadians’ minds: Can Trump change the name of Lake Ontario?

“The short answer is yes and no,” Kapelos explained Thursday after Trump’s announcement.

“He can do what he wants as far as what the United States is able to, or wants to, or decides to call any body of water or any landmark,” she said.

“But he cannot dictate what Canadians call that body of water, or maybe more importantly … what the international community or other countries call it.”

Kayla Thompson, CTVNews.ca journalist

How did Lake Ontario get its name?

The name is older than Canada itself.

Historians believe Lake Ontario’s name has Iroquoian roots meaning “beautiful lake” or “sparkling water,” according to the Canadian Encyclopedia.

Europeans began calling the lake “Ontario” in 1641, the encyclopedia entry says, and by 1656 the name was appearing on maps.

The province of Ontario is named after the lake.

Read the full story here

U.S. Board of Geographic Names ordered to rename lake

U.S. Interior Secretary Doug Burgum issued an official order to the U.S. Board of Geographic Names to change the name of Lake Ontario to “Lake America.”

Burgum shared the order in a social media post on Thursday with the caption “Make the Great Lakes Great Again!”

“The area formally known as Lake Ontario has long been an integral asset to America, as a critical artery for America’s early trade and commerce, and as a vital economic resource for America,” the order said.

“President Trump has directed the change in the name of Lake Ontario to Lake America, and the BGN must immediately take steps to accomplish the President’s instructions,” the document read.

“This order is effective immediately.”

Kayla Thompson, CTVNews.ca journalist

Trump claims ‘Lake America’ name change official

Trump posted a letter on Truth Social which declared that Lake Ontario is now “Lake America.”

“As of 4:30 pm today the U.S. Geological Survey (USGS) has officially designated the former Lake Ontario to be renamed as Lake America in all official USGS electronic documents,” a letter from USGS director Ned Mamula read, which Trump posted on Truth Social.

The letter added that printed documents will reflect the change in “the next several days.”

Trump also posted a map with “Lake America” in large bold red letters highlighting Lake Ontario.

‘Not his best work’: Kinew on Trump

Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew responded to Trump’s renaming of Lake Ontario, telling reporters the move is not the U.S. president’s “best work.”

“You know when a rock band is really over the hill, and you see them in a casino playing some song from like 50 years ago?” he said. “I think that’s the part of Donald Trump’s presidency we’re at now.”

Kinew said Trump “thought he had a real hit, a real golden oldie,” when he renamed the Gulf of Mexico the “Gulf of America” in January 2025, and “he’s trying (to) bring back that and he’s trying to play the hits for his base.”

“But I think everybody here thinks it’s a little sad and it’s not his best work,” he added.

Kayla Thompson, CTVNews.ca journalist

Ontario’s Ford weighs in on Trump order

Ontario Premier Doug Ford weighed in on Trump’s renaming of Lake Ontario, echoing what Carney and other Canadian politicians have said.

“It’s Lake Ontario to Canadians and the rest of the world. Now and forever,” Ford wrote in a post on social media.

Earlier this week, during an appearance on Bloomberg TV, Ford said it was up to Trump if he wanted to change it, but Canadians will “always going to call it Lake Ontario.”

Bryann Aguilar, CP24.com journalist

‘They feel entitled’ Trump says about Canada

When asked by reporters why he’s so focused on America’s ally, Trump said “they haven’t treated us well.”

“The Canadian officials have treated us very badly. They’re nasty people. They charge our farmers 400 per cent tariffs,” Trump responded.

“People oftentimes, they’ll ask me who’s the worst to deal with… and I said that’s easy: Canada. They are the worst, and they feel entitled, and just we can’t have that.”

Kayla Thompson, CTVNews.ca journalist

Trump: Canada ‘ripping us off for a long time’

When asked what message Trump is attempting to send to Canada with the renaming, the president reiterated that Canada has been “ripping us off for a long time on trade.”

“Very sadly, even the military. You know, we defend Canada for nothing. We don’t get anything. They don’t pay us to defend Canada, but we defend Canada, and they understand that,” he told reporters.

Trump brought up 11 brand new icebreakers as an example of his grievances.

“They’d like to use the icebreakers. They don’t pay for anything, and they want to be treated like a state, but they’re not a state.”

Kayla Thompson, CTVNews.ca journalist

‘Do I care about how the Québécois speak?’ Lutnick says

U.S. Secretary of Commerce Howard Lutnick claims the U.S. did not raise issues with the French language or the Québécois in trade negotiation talks with Canada last week.

“If you think I ever said the words ‘French,’ do I care about how the Quebecois speak?” he said to reporters in Washington on Thursday.

“I mean, what could matter less to America? We don’t care. So, the fact is, we never brought those words up.”

Lutnick claims the detail was “manufactured” by Prime Minister Mark Carney to end negotiations with the U.S.

“There’s the sovereignty party trying to run, and they’re in the lead in Quebec, and so this was Mark manufacturing something that would try to keep them from winning.”

Kayla Thompson, CTVNews.ca journalist

‘The math was sensational’: Lutnick

“We’re just being used by them,” Lutnick told reporters about Canada’s decision to end trade talks.

“That’s why it ended. It didn’t happen for math. The math was sensational,” he said. “It was a great deal that we shook hands on.”

Lutnick also claimed that concerns about medium- to heavy-duty trucks were strategically held by Canada until the last moment in trade negotiations.

Despite meeting with LeBlanc 10 times and speaking to Carney twice, “the words ‘medium’ and ‘heavy-duty trucks’ were raised in these trade negotiations at Friday at 4:00,” he added.

“These were things they put in in order to make it end,” he said.

Kayla Thompson, CTVNews.ca journalist

Canada replacing seafood counter-tariffs with other items

The federal government is replacing its counter-tariffs on seafood with 50 per cent levies on a series of other American goods, according to Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne’s office.

“This decision was made in the interest of strengthening Canada’s sectors and our tariff response — and to better match the American tariffs dollar for dollar, rate for rate,” Champagne’s press secretary John Fragos wrote in a statement to CTV News, adding the federal government has been consulting with stakeholders and provinces when it comes to counter-tariff options.

Fragos also tells CTV News that the decision to remove seafood from Canada’s list of counter-tariffs was made in part to avoid giving the appearance of escalation by Canada in the face of a simmering trade conflict with the United States, as the U.S. does not tariff Canadian seafood imports.

Newly added to Canada’s list of counter-tariffs include:

  • Wood charcoal;
  • Printed matter, including printed pictures or photographs;
  • Articles of plaster or of compositions based on plaster, including boards, sheets and tiles;
  • Materials used in the conveyance or packing of goods, including bottles, flasks, jars and pots;
  • And copper wire.

Spencer Van Dyk, CTV News writer & producer and Stephanie Ha, CTV News Ottawa National Bureau manager

items._ogDesc: Cale Makar and the Colorado Avalanche agreed to a US$163.2 million, eight-year extension on Friday that will make him the highest paid player in league history.
items.body:
DENVER — Cale Makar and the Colorado Avalanche agreed to a US$163.2 million, eight-year extension on Friday that will make him the highest paid player in league history.

The terms of the deal were confirmed by his agency, Bartlett Hockey.

Makar’s extension is set to be the the richest in NHL history, surpassing the eight-year, $136 million extension signed by Minnesota forward Kirill Kaprizov last September. Makar’s deal runs through the 2034-35 season.

With an annual average value (AAV) of $20.4 million beginning in 2027-28, Makar’s deal eclipses that of San Jose Sharks superstar Macklin Celebrini, who signed a five-year, $94 million extension in late July and has an $18.8 million AAV.

Makar’s record-setting deal could push the limit even higher with Edmonton’s Connor McDavid and Toronto’s Auston Matthews eligible for extensions next summer.

“I couldn’t be more excited to continue my journey here with the Avalanche in this amazing city of Denver,” Makar said in a video posted on social media by the team, calling it a historic day. “Here’s to another hopefully amazing nine years.”

The 27-year-old Makar is coming off a season in which he had 20 goals and 59 assists. He finished second to Zach Werenski of Columbus in the Norris Trophy voting, an award that goes to the league’s top defenceman. Makar has won the award twice over his career.

The cap hit for Makar for last season was $9 million after signing a six-year, $54 million contract in 2021. The new deal for Makar now sets the bar for fellow standout defencemen Quinn Hughes of Minnesota and Werenski.

Securing the long-term services of Makar was a high priority this offseason for president of hockey operations/general manager Joe Sakic, who maintained that Makar was “going to finish his career” in Colorado. Makar was taken fourth overall by Colorado in 2017 out of the University of Massachusetts.

The salary cap is projected to be $113.5 million in 2027-28 when Makar’s new deal begins. He will take up roughly 18 per cent of the room for a team with a Cup-ready roster. Left wing Artturi Lehkonen is set to be a free agent after this season, along with center Nicolas Roy and goaltender Scott Wedgewood.

Makar was banged up heading into a Western Conference Final where the Presidents’ Trophy-winning Avalanche were swept by the Vegas Golden Knights. An upper-body injury sidelined him for Games 1 and 2, but he returned for the final two contests. Sakic recently said that Makar is slated to be ready for training camp.

It’s been a busy offseason for Sakic, who’s stepping back into the role of GM after Chris MacFarland left to lead the front office in Nashville. Among the deals orchestrated by Sakic was sending Valeri Nichushkin to the Blue Jackets for draft picks. It was a way to free up space to negotiate the extension for Makar.

A native of Calgary, Makar has turned in four 20-goal seasons in his career, one of just 12 defencemen in league history to post at least that many campaigns. He also notched his 500th NHL point on March 28 in his 467th career game. He’s the fourth-fastest defenceman to reach that milestone, behind only Hall of Famers Bobby Orr (396 games), Paul Coffey (422) and Denis Potvin (465).

The core of Makar, Nathan MacKinnon and captain Gabriel Landeskog helped Colorado to a Stanley Cup title in 2022. Makar had eight goals and 21 assists during the championship run to capture the Conn Smythe Trophy as the MVP of the playoffs.

Makar’s younger brother, Taylor, recently signed a two-year contract with the Avalanche that runs through the 2027-28 season. Taylor Makar made his NHL debut on Nov. 1 in San Jose, as the brothers became the first siblings to appear in the same contest while playing for the Avalanche. The Stastny brothers -- Anton, Peter and Marian -- accomplished the feat when the team was the Quebec Nordiques.

AP hockey writers Stephen Whyno and John Wawrow contributed to this report.

Pat Graham, The Associated Press

TORONTO — Canada’s main stock index slid almost 300 points on Friday despite the latest GDP report pointing to a strengthening economy as trade tensions prevail. 

“I know that GDP was strong, but I think there are fears on both sides of the border about renewed tariffs or trade tensions, if you will, in terms of what could come next and the tit-for-tat that’s going on,” said Carol Schleif, chief market strategist at BMO Wealth Management.

But Schleif suggested taking late-summer Friday’s market moves with a grain of salt.

“It’s going to be hard to read too much long-term out of what the markets are doing in the afternoon on a Friday in the summer,” she said.

“Trading tends to be late; a lot of people are on vacation.”

The S&P/TSX composite index was down 280.33 points at 36,553.92.

  • Real-time TSX market updates here

In New York, the Dow Jones industrial average was down 9.45 points at 53,559.99. The S&P 500 index was down 19.23 points at 7,711.76, while the Nasdaq composite was down 138.93 points at 26,402.42.

Schleif said markets on both sides of the border are also unpacking U.S. Federal Reserve chair Kevin Warsh’s commentary at the economic symposium in Jackson Hole, Wyo., on Friday.

In his first high-profile speech, Warsh said inflation is still too high in the U.S., signalling that the Fed may have to raise interest rates in the coming months to bring it down. The U.S. bond markets jumped on the potential for a September rate hike.

“For the most part, it gave the market a little more grit in terms of what it had been looking for,” Schleif said.

Overall, she said the Jackson Hole Symposium appeared positive for the U.S. and Canada.

“There’s a really nice picture with Tiff Macklem and Warsh — they’re looking very friendly,” she said. “It’s always good when the people on the front lines making policy are on good terms.” 

Meanwhile, Bank of Canada governor Macklem will be up next week with his latest decision on interest rates, shortly after trade talks between Canada and the United States fell apart.

The United States imposed 50 per cent tariffs on roughly five per cent of Canadian exports on Aug. 22, and Canada plans to retaliate with its own counter-tariffs starting Sept. 8. 

The Canadian central bank has kept its benchmark rate on hold at 2.25 per cent for nearly a year now, and a broader consensus among economists is signalling another rate hold.

While the economy could slow with a prolonged trade dispute, Schleif said the TSX isn’t going to be affected by tariffs as much, considering its composition.

“The TSX is moving based on miners and financials and things that tend to be in pretty good stead and are benefiting from the fact that you had 3.3 per cent GDP growth,” she said.

Statistics Canada reported real gross domestic product rose 3.3 per cent in the second quarter on an annualized basis — the fastest pace in more than three years as exports and business capital investment ramped up.

Schleif said investors have so far remained resilient despite the geopolitical backdrop, with the TSX’s year-to-date return tallying 15 per cent.

items._ogDesc: Vaping company Juul Labs on Friday received federal permission to sell an updated version of its e-cigarette, which includes an optional age-verification system designed to prevent underage use.
items.body:
WASHINGTON — Vaping company Juul Labs on Friday received federal permission to sell an updated version of its e-cigarette, which includes an optional age-verification system designed to prevent underage use.

The decision from the U.S. Food and Drug Administration allows the company to sell a new version of its top-selling vaping device for the first time since it launched more than a decade ago. In recent years, the company has had to lay off hundreds of employees while paying roughly US$3 billion to settle government and private lawsuits over teen use of its products.

Juul plans to market the new device under the brand name Juul2, along with updated versions of its tobacco- and menthol-flavoured cartridges. In 2019, the company discontinued several flavours, including mango, mint and creme, that drove most of its sales but were favored by teens.

In a statement Friday, Juul CEO K.C. Crosthwaite said the company plans to seek authorization for “a portfolio of flavours -- beyond tobacco and menthol -- that are targeted to adult nicotine consumers.”

The latest announcement is not an approval or endorsement, and people who do not smoke should not use Juul or any other e-cigarettes, according to regulators. The FDA decision means that smokers who switch completely to Juul can reduce their exposure to deadly carcinogens and other chemicals found in traditional cigarettes.

According to company studies reviewed by the FDA, between 20 per cent to 50 per cent of smokers who used Juul products were able to stop smoking at the end of six weeks. The rates of quitting varied based on which flavours were used.

The new device also gives users the option to require age verification via an online app before the e-cigarette can be unlocked.

The FDA has authorized a handful of e-cigarettes to help adult smokers quit or cut back on cigarettes. In May, the FDA OK’d the first fruit-flavoured electronic cigarettes intended for adult smokers. The approval represented a major policy shift and came after months of appeals to U.S. President Donald Trump from the vaping industry.

Juul is no longer the top-selling e-cigarette brand in the U.S. and trails Vuse, which is sold by tobacco giant Reynolds American. Reynolds also makes Camel and Newport cigarettes.

Teens have shifted away from Juul as part of a wider drop in vaping, according to federal figures. Teens who continue to vape mostly use unauthorized disposable e-cigarettes imported from China, which come in fruit and candy flavours.

items.title: Under-utilized Surrey industrial site set for job-intensive makeover
items.description: Former MEC distribution centre to host more than 400 auto-oriented jobs
items._ogDesc: Former MEC distribution centre to host more than 400 auto-oriented jobs
items.body:
Demand for large-format industrial space is driving Metro Vancouver’s industrial market this year, but a 16-acre site in Surrey is set for a makeover that will see multiple uses with a single focus deliver more than the usual logistics hub.

Surrey city council approved a rezoning application by Conwest Developments Ltd. in January that will see it develop a multi-tenant, mixed-use auto mall for OpenRoad Auto Group Ltd. on the former Mountain Equipment Company (MEC) distribution centre at 13340 76 Ave. in Surrey’s Newton area.

Servicing will begin later this year, with construction expected to start in 2027. A ceremonial groundbreaking took place on Aug. 28.

Completion is expected in early 2028, with Surrey Honda and Mercedes-Benz Surrey in line to be the first tenants of up to eight tenants in what’s been christened the Surrey Auto Loop.

“It will be anchored by our auto use, but we also envision mixed-use opportunity as well – whether that be retail, food and beverage, and perhaps some ancillary or adjacent type uses as well. We think that will enhance the appeal and the value of the development overall,” Christian Chia, CEO of OpenRoad Auto Group Ltd., told Western Investor.

OpenRoad’s real estate holding company, Multiland Pacific Hoildings Ltd., will be the owner and developer of the site, which it acquired from Conwest earlier this year.

“We needed sufficient scale, and in the Greater Vancouver region that’s becoming increasingly elusive,” Chia explained. “For us that meant at least 10 acres; this site in particular is 16.”

The site is also in an easily accessible location and growth-oriented area of Surrey, which itself was receptive to the project. Rezoning took just three and a half months.

“The Surrey Auto Loop is a major investment in Newton and another sign of the growth and opportunity we’re seeing across our city,” Surrey Mayor Brenda Locke said in a statement announcing the development. “It will create local jobs and bring new economic activity to the area.”

While OpenForm Properties, a sibling company to OpenRoad, undertakes residential and office projects, Chia said Conwest’s expertise has been invaluable in shepherding the Surrey project through the approvals process.

“Their knowledge of more industrial, commercial types of developments is outside our specialty,” he said. “We couldn’t have done it without them.”

It was also a good fit for Conwest, which acquired the property through a sale-leaseback agreement with MEC in 2021, following MEC's sale to Kingswood Capital in fall 2020. MEC vacated the premises in early 2024, and the property has been vacant since.

“We were moving through an approval process to develop it into different types of industrial,” said Ben Taddei, chief operating officer and partner with Conwest Developments Ltd. “We were looking at leasehold property, we were looking at strata, but during that process, Christian Chia came to the table and we ended up doing a deal with him.”

The match was the right one given the flux in Metro Vancouver’s industrial real estate market.

Newmark Canada reported market-wide vacancies declining to 3.2 per cent in the second quarter down from 3.3 per cent at the end of 2025. Surrey has been particularly active, with vacancies falling from 3 per cent to 2.3 per cent over the same period, and emerging as the single most active market for construction.

Yet demand for strata space remains limited and leasehold demand skews larger, with tenants typically requiring fewer workers than OpenRoad anticipates employing in its development.

“The real activity today in the industrial market is in big bay leasehold – distribution, warehouse etc – so that was one of the concepts that we were looking at doing; one big building or two medium-sized buildings,” Taddei said. “But at the end of the day it made sense for everybody to get behind the vision that Christian had.”

Sales, service, administrative, marketing and technology staff will be employed at the site, all good-paying jobs that will benefit from the amenities planned.

“We rezoned it to expand the zone to allow for automotive uses and ancillary retail, so it’s industrial with expanded uses, and I think that’s a good interim use,” Taddei said. “As things evolve in the world, we’ll see what the long-term is for industrial in the region.”

items._ogDesc: Canada's economy rebounded with 0.9% GDP growth in Q2. Temporary boosts from the Census and World Cup are masking underlying weakness.
items.body:
Canada’s economy rebounded last quarter, but will it last? Statistics Canada’s (StatCan) Gross domestic product (GDP) data shows growth in June. That helped Q2 close out with much higher growth than anticipated, a sharp change from Q1. However, the bump was due to temporary events, leaving questions whether it will persist to Q3.

Canadian GDP Grew 0.3% In June, A Third Month of Growth

Canadian GDP advanced 0.3% in June, rising for a third straight month. The agency notes 13 of 20 industrial sectors, suggesting this growth is broad. Goods producing industries contracted (-0.1%) as mining, quarrying, and oil and gas extraction cooled. Though that segment cooled after providing significant lift in the quarter.

The contraction was offset by a 0.4% expansion in service industries. That was driven by wholesale trade, retail trade, and public administration. Gas prices helped to create that retail growth, and the public sector boost is temporary.

Canadian GDP Growth Driven By Temporary Events

The recent GDP reports got a big boost from two temporary events, the Census and World Cup. Census 2026 is the force behind the 1.9% jump in federal government administration, driving public administration. We previously noted the Census likely padded employment, which this data confirms.

Canada hosting 10 World Cup matches got special attention from the agency in June. Not just for the lift it provided, but the areas where it didn’t surprised the agency. The GDP sector of information and cultural industries expanded (+0.4%) in June, largely due to broadcasting (+8.6%). Arts, entertainment and recreation (+1.1%) also rose, but only spectator sports grew. Public transit (+1.1%) increased too, attributed to the influx of tourists and spectators.

However, the World Cup boost didn’t help industries related to tourism. Accommodation service (-0.7%) and air transportation (-0.5%) both declined. This suggests the climb may have cannibalized typical tourist streams.

Real Estate Extends Its GDP Winning Streak, Fueled By Ontario

The real estate industry has been on a winning streak in terms of GDP growth. Real estate and rental and leasing grew 0.2% in June, marking a fifth straight month of growth. It got a big jump from the sub-sector of real estate agents and brokers, which expanded 0.6% in the month. This was largely attributed to growth in Ontario.

June Spike Helps Push Q2 GDP Towards Healthy Growth Levels

Canadian GDP Q2 2026: Growth by sector.

The end of the month also wrapped up the quarter, which saw GDP advance 0.9% in Q2. This follows Q1’s sluggish 0.1% growth, as the energy sector supercharged the first two months of the quarter. More specifically, mining, quarrying, and oil and gas extraction (+2.2%) was lifted by global demand.

Canadian GDP came in stronger than many had anticipated, but it’s not in the clear—nor is it clear if the growth will last. The bulk of the growth is driven by temporary factors that won’t be repeated. Temporary events can help revive an economy, but it’s too early to tell if the drag in Q1 or the growth in Q2 is the passing phase.
